title: The Second Declension — Neuter
subtitle: τὸ δῶρον, τὸ τέκνον — and the neuter plural rule.
objectives: Decline any second-declension neuter noun in all five cases and both numbers.
Apply the neuter plural rule: neuter plural subjects take singular verbs.
Recognize that nominative and accusative are always identical in the neuter.
Parse second-declension neuter nouns on sight.

sections.heading: The neuter
sections.body:
Neuter nouns of the second declension end in -ον in the nominative singular. They follow the same pattern as the masculine nouns in the genitive and dative, but the nominative and accusative are always identical. This is true in the singular and in the plural.

The neuter plural nominative and accusative end in -α. This looks like a feminine singular ending, but it is not. τὰ δῶρα is neuter plural: 'the gifts'.

The neuter plural rule is absolute: a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb. τὰ τέκνα τρέχει means 'the children run', not τρέχουσιν. This rule applies to all neuter nouns in Greek, not just the second declension.

sections.heading: The paradigm: τὸ δῶρον (gift)
sections.body:
singular        plural
  nominative  δῶρον           δῶρα
  genitive    δώρου           δώρων
  dative      δώρῳ            δώροις
  accusative  δῶρον           δῶρα
  vocative    δῶρον           δῶρα

With the article:
  nominative  τὸ δῶρον        τὰ δῶρα
  genitive    τοῦ δώρου       τῶν δώρων
  dative      τῷ δώρῳ         τοῖς δώροις
  accusative  τὸ δῶρον        τὰ δῶρα
  vocative    ὦ δῶρον         ὦ δῶρα

Notice: nominative, accusative, and vocative are identical in both numbers.

sections.heading: The neuter plural rule in action
sections.body:
τὰ τέκνα τρέχει. 'The children run.' (singular verb)
τὰ δῶρα καλά ἐστιν. 'The gifts are beautiful.' (singular verb ἐστιν)

This rule feels strange to an English speaker. In English, 'the children run', not 'the children runs'. But in Greek, neuter plural subjects are treated as collective singulars. The rule is universal and never has exceptions.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 2.4 introduces the first declension feminine nouns ending in -η: ἡ ἀρετή, ἡ τιμή, ἡ τέχνη. The first declension is more varied than the second, with three sub-types depending on the vowel in the stem. We begin with the most regular type.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can decline any second-declension neuter noun from memory and can correctly apply the neuter plural rule in at least five example sentences.
